web_evidence.title: Read the book: The Mandarins
web_evidence.note: The authorized HarperCollins ebook excerpt provides sustained Chapter One narration centered externally on Henri, consistently using he/him while reporting his actions and thoughts.

web_evidence.title: Alex Woloch: Bleak House: 19, 20, 21
web_evidence.note: This peer-reviewed essay identifies The Mandarins as a novel whose persistent narrative voices occupy first- and third-person modes and alternate without a master frame.

web_evidence.title: Experience of Our Time
web_evidence.note: The contemporary review explicitly says the point of view changes in alternate chapters from third to first, identifying Henri as the focus of the third-person plot and Anne as the first-person narrator.

web_evidence.title: A Political Novel
web_evidence.note: A transcribed 1957 International Socialist Review article describes each chapter as containing a first-person section told by Anne and a third-person section centered mainly on Henri.

person_note: The novel has two sustained base modes: Anne Dubreuilh narrates her sections as a participating first-person I, while Henri Perron's sections use third-person narration. The quotes repeatedly expose Anne's base voice, especially q00595, q00604, and q00606, and contain third-person beats consistent with Henri's strand. Short isolated she/he passages were conservatively left unmarked. The authorized opening independently demonstrates Henri's third-person mode, while whole-book structural sources explicitly establish persistent alternation between Anne's first-person and Henri's third-person sections. Some quote snippets lack section labels, but the independent structural evidence resolves that limited uncertainty.
